courses.title: Market Foundations
courses.description: Start here. Plain-language trading terms, what markets are, how to read a candlestick and its most common patterns, how timeframes work, and how to read trend, range and key levels on a chart.

lessons.title: Trading Terms Every Beginner Needs to Know

slides.heading: A shorthand worth learning
slides.body: Every new field has its own vocabulary, and trading is no different. This lesson covers the handful of plain-language terms you'll see again and again — learn them once here, in one place, so nothing later on has to stop and explain itself.

slides.heading: Pip
slides.body: A pip is the smallest standard unit price is usually measured in — on most currency pairs, the 4th decimal place. If EUR/USD moves from 1.1000 to 1.1010, it moved 10 pips. It's the 'inch' or 'centimetre' of price movement.

slides.heading: Bid, Ask & Spread
slides.body: The Bid is the price you can sell at right now. The Ask is the price you can buy at right now. The Ask is always slightly higher — that small gap is the spread, a built-in cost on every trade, paid to whoever is making the market.

slides.heading: Long vs Short
slides.body: Going long means buying first, expecting the price to rise so you can sell it later for more. Going short means selling first, expecting the price to fall so you can buy it back later for less. Both directions are always available.

quiz.question: What is a pip?
options: A type of candlestick
The smallest standard unit price is measured in
A trading fee charged by brokers
The name of a chart pattern
quiz.explanation: A pip is the standard smallest unit of price movement — on most pairs, the 4th decimal place.

quiz.question: What is the spread?
options: A bonus paid to winning traders
The gap between the Bid (sell) price and the Ask (buy) price
Another name for leverage
The total number of pips in a day
quiz.explanation: The spread is the small gap between the price you can sell at (Bid) and the price you can buy at (Ask) — a built-in cost on every trade.

quiz.question: You expect a currency pair's price to fall and want to profit from that. What do you do?
options: Go long (buy first)
Go short (sell first)
Wait — you can only ever buy
Increase your leverage
quiz.explanation: Going short means selling first, expecting to buy it back later at a lower price — the way to profit from an expected decline.

slides.heading: Markets, in one sentence
slides.body: A financial market is a place where people agree on a price to exchange something — a currency, a company's shares, a commodity like gold — either right now or for future delivery.

slides.heading: The four markets in TradeWise
slides.body: Forex (currency pairs like EUR/USD), Metals (gold, silver), Crypto (BTC, ETH), and Stocks (company shares). TradeWise starts you on Forex — EUR/USD specifically — because it's deep, liquid, and its chart behaviour is the clearest to learn confluence from.

slides.heading: Who's on the other side of your trade
slides.body: Banks, hedge funds, corporations hedging currency exposure, and other retail traders. You are never trading against an abstract 'market' — every trade has a real counterparty taking the opposite side.

slides.heading: Why price actually moves
slides.body: Simplified supply and demand: more buyers than sellers at a price pushes it up, more sellers than buyers pushes it down. Everything else you learn in this app is about reading the visible footprints of that imbalance on a chart.

quiz.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four market types covered in TradeWise?
options: Forex
Stocks
Real Estate
Crypto
quiz.explanation: Real estate investing lives in the separate PropWise app. TradeWise covers Forex, Metals, Crypto, and Stocks.

quiz.question: Why does TradeWise start you on Forex specifically?
options: It never loses value
It has deep liquidity and the clearest chart behaviour to learn from
It doesn't involve real prices
It requires no risk management
quiz.explanation: Forex — and EUR/USD in particular — is deep and liquid, which produces cleaner, more learnable chart structure than thinner markets.

quiz.question: What fundamentally moves price in a market?
options: Government announcements only
The balance of buyers and sellers at a given price
Random chance
The app's internal algorithm
quiz.explanation: Price is the visible result of supply and demand — more buyers than sellers pushes price up, and vice versa.

slides.heading: What one candle represents
slides.body: A single candlestick shows four numbers for a fixed time window: Open, High, Low, Close (OHLC). The 'body' spans open-to-close; the thin 'wicks' show the high and low reached during that window.

slides.heading: Bullish vs bearish
slides.body: A bullish (typically green) candle closes higher than it opened — buyers won that window. A bearish (typically red) candle closes lower than it opened — sellers won.

slides.heading: What a long wick tells you
slides.body: A long wick means price reached further in that direction but got rejected and closed back the other way — a visible sign that side lost control before the window closed.

quiz.question: What does the 'body' of a candlestick represent?
options: The highest and lowest price reached
The range between the open and close price
The trading volume
The next candle's likely direction
quiz.explanation: The body spans from the open price to the close price. The wicks (thin lines) show the high and low reached during the window.

quiz.question: A candle opens at 1.1000 and closes at 1.0950. What is it?
options: Bullish
Bearish
Neutral
A doji
quiz.explanation: It closed lower than it opened, so sellers won that window — that's a bearish candle.

quiz.question: A candle has a long upper wick and a small body near the bottom. What does that suggest?
options: Buyers pushed price up and held it there
Price pushed higher but was rejected and closed back down
The candle has no meaningful information
Volume was zero
quiz.explanation: A long upper wick with the close near the low means buyers tried to push price up during the window but were rejected — sellers regained control before the close.

slides.heading: Marubozu — full conviction
slides.body: A long body with almost no wick on either end. Open and close sit right at the extremes — one side controlled the entire window, start to finish, with no meaningful pushback.

slides.heading: Doji — pure indecision
slides.body: Open and close are nearly identical, even though price may have moved noticeably in both directions during the window. Neither buyers nor sellers won — it's a dead heat.

slides.heading: Spinning Top — a tug of war
slides.body: A small body with long wicks on both sides. Price pushed meaningfully higher and lower before settling near where it started — real disagreement, no clear winner.

quiz.question: What defines a Marubozu candle?
options: A tiny body with long wicks both sides
A long body with almost no wick on either end
Open and close are nearly equal
It only appears on the 1H timeframe
quiz.explanation: A Marubozu has almost no wick — the body runs nearly the full high-to-low range, showing one side in complete control.

quiz.question: What does a Doji tell you?
options: One side was in total control
Neither side won — open and close are nearly equal despite price moving both ways
The market is closed
Price broke a key level
quiz.explanation: A Doji shows a dead heat — open and close land almost exactly together, even if price wandered during the window.

quiz.question: A candle has a small body with long wicks on both the top and bottom. What is it?
options: Marubozu
Doji
Spinning Top
Bullish engulfing
quiz.explanation: That's a Spinning Top — real pushes in both directions, but neither side held on by the close.

slides.heading: One candle is a hint, not a story
slides.body: A chart is a sequence of candles read left to right. Any single candle's shape only becomes meaningful once you know what came before it — the same shape can mean something different depending on context.

slides.heading: What turns a shape into a formation
slides.body: A formation is a specific candle shape (or small group of candles) appearing in a specific place — usually after a clear prior trend. A hammer shape after a decline is a formation; the exact same shape in the middle of a flat range isn't telling you much.

slides.heading: Single-candle formations vs multi-candle formations
slides.body: Some formations are a single candle read against the prior trend (like a hammer or shooting star). Others need two or three candles working together (like an engulfing pattern or a star pattern). Both types are covered next.

quiz.question: Why does the same candle shape mean different things in different places on a chart?
options: It doesn't — shape alone always means the same thing
A formation depends on context, especially the trend leading into it
Only the most recent candle ever matters
Candle shapes are decorative and carry no information
quiz.explanation: Context is what turns a shape into a signal — the same hammer shape means something different after a decline than in the middle of a flat range.

quiz.question: What is a formation, as distinct from a single candle shape?
options: Any random candle on the chart
A specific shape (or small group of candles) appearing in a specific place, usually after a clear prior trend
A candle with high trading volume
A candle that appears on the Daily timeframe only
quiz.explanation: A formation is a shape plus context — most commonly, that shape appearing right after a clear trend has been established.

quiz.question: Which of these is a multi-candle formation, needing two or three candles working together?
options: A single hammer
A single shooting star
An engulfing pattern
A single Marubozu
quiz.explanation: An engulfing pattern is defined by two candles together — one body swallowing the other. Hammer, shooting star, and Marubozu are all single-candle formations.

slides.heading: Bullish Engulfing
slides.body: After a decline, a bearish candle is immediately followed by a larger bullish candle whose body fully swallows the prior one. It signals buyers have decisively taken over.

slides.heading: Bearish Engulfing
slides.body: The mirror image: after an advance, a bullish candle is immediately followed by a larger bearish candle whose body fully swallows it. Sellers have decisively taken over.

slides.heading: Hammer
slides.body: After a decline, a candle with a small body and a long lower wick — price pushed well below, then buyers rejected the lower prices and closed back up near the open.

slides.heading: Shooting Star
slides.body: After an advance, a candle with a small body and a long upper wick — price pushed well above, then sellers rejected the higher prices and closed back down near the open.

slides.heading: Morning Star
slides.body: A 3-candle reversal after a decline: a big bearish candle, a small indecisive candle, then a big bullish candle — the market's mood visibly turning from selling to buying.

slides.heading: Evening Star
slides.body: The mirror image after an advance: a big bullish candle, a small indecisive candle, then a big bearish candle — the mood turning from buying to selling.

quiz.question: After a decline, a bearish candle is followed by a larger bullish candle whose body fully swallows it. What pattern is this?
options: Bearish Engulfing
Bullish Engulfing
Shooting Star
Evening Star
quiz.explanation: That's a Bullish Engulfing pattern — the larger bullish body fully swallowing the prior bearish body after a decline.

quiz.question: A candle after a decline has a small body and a long lower wick. What is it?
options: Shooting Star
Hammer
Bearish Engulfing
Marubozu
quiz.explanation: A Hammer — small body, long lower wick, appearing after a decline, signals a rejection of lower prices.

quiz.question: Big bearish candle → small indecisive candle → big bullish candle, after a decline. What pattern is this?
options: Evening Star
Morning Star
Bearish Engulfing
Spinning Top
quiz.explanation: That three-candle sequence — bearish, indecisive, bullish — after a decline is a Morning Star, one of the clearest reversal signals covered here.

slides.heading: What a timeframe is
slides.body: Each timeframe (5M, 15M, 1H, 4H, D1) sets how much time one candle covers. A 5-minute (5M) candle covers 5 minutes of trading; a Daily (D1) candle covers a full day.

slides.heading: Zooming out for context, zooming in for precision
slides.body: Higher timeframes (1H, 4H) show the bigger trend and the key levels that matter. Lower timeframes (5M) show the precise moment to act. TradeWise's core mechanic uses 5M for decisions, with 1H available as context.

slides.heading: Why TradeWise pauses before you decide
slides.body: The chart pauses at a 5M decision point before you commit — not after price has already moved. This is the single most important habit this app is built to train: deciding under uncertainty, not labelling in hindsight.

quiz.question: What does a '1H' candle represent?
options: 1 hour of price action
1 trade
100 candles
1 day
quiz.explanation: 1H means each candle on that chart covers one hour of trading.

quiz.question: Why would you check a higher timeframe like 1H before acting on a 5M setup?
options: You wouldn't — lower timeframes are always sufficient alone
To see the bigger trend and key levels that give the 5M setup context
Because 5M charts are inaccurate
To slow down your internet connection
quiz.explanation: A higher timeframe shows the broader trend and major levels — context that tells you whether a 5M setup is trading with or against the bigger picture.

quiz.question: Why does the chart pause before you commit to a trade in TradeWise?
options: To save battery
Because that's how live trading works — you always see the outcome first
To force a real decision under uncertainty, not a hindsight judgement
It's a loading screen, nothing more
quiz.explanation: TradeWise's core mechanic is pre-hoc: you commit direction, size, SL and TP before the outcome plays out — the same conditions as real trading.

slides.heading: Uptrend
slides.body: A series of higher highs and higher lows. Each pullback finds a floor above the last one — buyers are progressively more willing to pay more.

slides.heading: Downtrend
slides.body: A series of lower highs and lower lows — the mirror image. Each rally fails below the last one.

slides.heading: Range
slides.body: Price oscillates between a repeated ceiling and floor with no clear higher-highs/higher-lows or lower-highs/lower-lows progression. Neither side is in control yet.

quiz.question: What defines an uptrend?
options: Equal highs and equal lows
A series of higher highs and higher lows
Any green candle
Price moving sideways
quiz.explanation: An uptrend is specifically a pattern of higher highs and higher lows — each pullback holding above the prior low.

quiz.question: What defines a downtrend?
options: A series of higher highs and higher lows
A series of lower highs and lower lows
Price bouncing in a flat range
Any red candle
quiz.explanation: A downtrend is a series of lower highs and lower lows — the mirror image of an uptrend, with each rally failing below the last one.

quiz.question: Price is bouncing between the same ceiling and floor with no clear higher-highs/higher-lows pattern. What structure is this?
options: Uptrend
Downtrend
Range
Compression breakout
quiz.explanation: That's a range — neither buyers nor sellers have taken clear control, so price oscillates between a repeated ceiling and floor.

slides.heading: Key levels, defined
slides.body: A support level is a floor price has bounced off more than once. A resistance level is a ceiling price has been rejected from more than once. These are the levels every confluence setup in Course 2 is built around.

slides.heading: Support in context
slides.body: Support usually shows up after a decline — price falls toward a level and buyers step back in, at least twice, before you can call it a real floor.

slides.heading: Resistance in context
slides.body: Resistance usually shows up after an advance — price rises toward a level and sellers step back in, at least twice, before you can call it a real ceiling.

quiz.question: What is a support level?
options: A price ceiling price has been rejected from repeatedly
A price floor price has bounced off repeatedly
The opening price of the day
A random horizontal line
quiz.explanation: Support is a floor — a price where buying pressure has repeatedly stepped in and held price up.

quiz.question: What is a resistance level?
options: A price floor price has bounced off repeatedly
A price ceiling price has been rejected from repeatedly
The closing price of the day
The same thing as a support level
quiz.explanation: Resistance is a ceiling — a price where selling pressure has repeatedly stepped in and turned price back down.

quiz.question: Why do support and resistance levels matter so much for the confluence setups in Course 2?
options: They don't — Course 2 ignores levels entirely
Every core setup is built around price reacting at a key level, not just a candlestick pattern in isolation
They only matter on the Daily timeframe
They guarantee a reversal every time price touches them
quiz.explanation: Course 2's setups all combine a key level with a confirming signal — levels are the 'where', candlestick patterns are the 'what', and neither is enough alone.

items.explanation: It closed above where it opened, with wicks on both sides that aren't extreme enough to call it a Marubozu — just a plain bullish candle.
It closed below where it opened — a plain bearish candle.
Open and close are nearly identical despite wicks on both sides — that's the definition of a Doji, indecision rather than a directional read.
It closed above where it opened (bullish) with almost no wick on either end (Marubozu) — both labels are genuinely true here.
The small body sits inside long wicks on both sides — the real story is the tug of war, not the tiny directional lean of the body.
Each swing high and swing low is higher than the last — that's an uptrend.
Each swing high and swing low is lower than the last — that's a downtrend.
Price is oscillating between the same two levels with no higher-highs/higher-lows or lower-highs/lower-lows progression.
Price fell into the level (a downtrend) before finding buyers there more than once — both labels apply to this chart at once.
Price rose into the level (an uptrend) before being turned back there more than once — both labels apply to this chart at once.
Each candle here spans 5 minutes, and the sequence is also climbing in higher highs and higher lows — both labels are true together.
Each candle here spans 1 hour, used for context, and it's also showing a clear uptrend — both labels are true together.
A bullish body fully swallowing the prior bearish body, right after a decline — a textbook Bullish Engulfing.
Big bearish candle, small indecisive candle, big bullish candle, after a decline — the three-candle Morning Star reversal.

courses.title: Confluence & Setups
courses.description: Why one signal is never enough, and the first three of TradeWise's five core confluence setups — plus how to spot the traps designed to look like them.

slides.heading: One signal is never enough
slides.body: A confluence is two or more independent signals agreeing on direction at the same time and place. A candlestick pattern alone, or a level alone, is not a trade — TradeWise never scores a single signal as sufficient.

slides.heading: Why this matters
slides.body: Markets are noisy. Any one signal produces false positives constantly. Requiring agreement between independent signals is what filters noise from a genuine edge.

slides.heading: The 5 core setups, at a glance
slides.body: Across this course and the Advanced course you'll learn 5 confluence setups: Key Level + Candlestick, Trend + Fibonacci Retracement, Structure Break + Retest, Multi-Timeframe Confluence, and Compression Breakout. This course covers the first three.

slides.heading: What separates a valid setup from a trap
slides.body: A trap looks like a setup at first glance but is missing a component, or one component actively contradicts another. Spotting traps is as much a skill as spotting valid setups — Lesson 5 is built entirely around it.

quiz.question: What is a confluence?
options: Any single candlestick pattern
Two or more independent signals agreeing on direction
A type of chart timeframe
The opening price of the trading day
quiz.explanation: A confluence requires two or more independent signals pointing the same direction — never just one.

quiz.question: Why does TradeWise require multiple agreeing signals instead of trading off one?
options: Because a single signal produces too many false positives on its own
Because the app is designed to reduce how often you trade for its own sake
Single signals are against the rules of the game
It doesn't — one clean signal is always enough
quiz.explanation: Any one signal alone is noisy and unreliable. Requiring agreement between independent signals filters out much of that noise.

quiz.question: How many core confluence setups does TradeWise teach in total (Course 2 + the Advanced course)?
quiz.explanation: There are 5 core setups total — 3 covered in this course, and 2 more (Multi-Timeframe Confluence and Compression Breakout) in the Advanced course.

slides.heading: The two components
slides.body: Component A: price is at a key level (support or resistance) with at least 2 prior touches. Component B: a reversal candlestick forms right at that level — bullish engulfing, bearish engulfing, pin bar, hammer, or shooting star.

slides.heading: Valid buy / valid sell
slides.body: Valid BUY: a touch of support plus a bullish engulfing or pin bar at the level. Valid SELL: a touch of resistance plus a bearish engulfing or shooting star at the level.

slides.heading: The trap version
slides.body: Price approaches the level but the confirming candle is a doji or has an ambiguous body — no clean directional signal. The correct call is No Trade, not a guess.

quiz.question: What are the two components of Setup 1?
options: A key level and a reversal candlestick at that level
Two moving averages crossing
High volume and a news event
A Fibonacci level and RSI reading
quiz.explanation: Setup 1 is a key level (support/resistance with 2+ prior touches) plus a reversal candlestick confirming right at that level.

quiz.question: Price touches resistance and a bearish engulfing candle forms right at the level. What's the valid call?
options: Buy
Sell
No Trade — needs a third signal
Wait for a doji
quiz.explanation: Resistance + bearish engulfing at the level is exactly the valid SELL version of Setup 1.

quiz.question: Price touches support but the candle at the level is a doji. What's the correct call?
options: Buy — support always holds
Sell — doji means reversal
No Trade — no clean confirming candle
Buy with a wider stop
quiz.explanation: A doji shows indecision, not a confirming reversal candle. Without a clean Component B, this is the trap version — No Trade is correct.

slides.heading: The components
slides.body: Component A: a clear 1H trend (3+ swing points confirming direction). Component B: price retraces to the 50% or 61.8% Fibonacci level of the most recent impulse move on the 5M chart. Component C (optional, strengthens the setup): a candlestick confirmation right at the Fib level.

slides.heading: Valid buy / valid sell
slides.body: Valid BUY: 1H uptrend, pullback to the 50%/61.8% Fib level, plus a bullish candle. Valid SELL: 1H downtrend, retrace to the 50%/61.8% Fib level, plus a bearish candle.

slides.heading: The trap version
slides.body: Price hits the Fib level, but the 1H trend is actually ranging, not trending — there's no higher-timeframe context to trade with. Correct call: No Trade.

quiz.question: Which Fibonacci levels does this setup use?
quiz.explanation: Setup 2 looks for a retracement to the 50% or 61.8% Fibonacci level of the most recent impulse.

quiz.question: What is Component A of Setup 2, and why does it matter?
options: Trading volume — it filters low-liquidity moves
A clear 1H trend — it gives the retracement a direction to continue
A round number price level
The time of day
quiz.explanation: Without a clear higher-timeframe trend, a retracement to a Fib level has nothing to continue — that's what makes it valid rather than a coin flip.

quiz.question: Price hits the 61.8% Fib level, but the 1H chart is ranging rather than trending. What's the correct call?
options: Buy — Fib levels always hold
Sell — ranging means reversal
No Trade — there's no trend for the retracement to continue
Wait for volume to increase
quiz.explanation: Component A (a clear 1H trend) is missing. Without it, this is the trap version — No Trade is correct.

slides.heading: The components
slides.body: Component A: a clear break of a prior swing high (for a buy) or swing low (for a sell) on the 5M chart, closing beyond it by 10+ pips. Component B: price returns to retest the broken level. Component C: a candlestick confirmation at the retest.

slides.heading: Valid buy / valid sell
slides.body: Valid BUY: prior resistance breaks, price retests it from above, and a bullish confirmation candle forms. Valid SELL: prior support breaks, price retests from below, and a bearish confirmation candle forms.

slides.heading: The trap version — false break
slides.body: Price breaks the level, but on the 'retest' it aggressively pushes straight back through and continues past — that's not a retest, it's a false break (liquidity sweep). Correct call: No Trade.

quiz.question: What has to happen before Setup 3 is even in play?
options: A clear break of a prior swing high or low, closing beyond it
A doji at a support level
Three consecutive green candles
The 1H timeframe must be ranging
quiz.explanation: Setup 3 starts with a genuine structure break — a close beyond a prior swing high/low by 10+ pips — before the retest is even relevant.

quiz.question: After a break of resistance, what confirms a valid retest entry?
options: Any touch of the old level
Price retesting the broken level from above with a bullish confirmation candle
Price immediately reversing through the level and continuing
A gap in the chart
quiz.explanation: The retest needs to hold from the correct side (above, after a resistance break) and get a confirming candle — that's what makes it a valid Setup 3 entry, not just a random touch.

quiz.question: Price breaks support, then aggressively pushes back up through the level and keeps going. What is this?
options: A textbook valid retest
A false break / liquidity sweep — the trap version
Setup 2 in disguise
Guaranteed continuation downward
quiz.explanation: This is the trap version of Setup 3 — the 'retest' is actually a false break. The correct read is No Trade, not treating it as a valid retest.

slides.heading: Why traps exist in this curriculum
slides.body: Real markets don't announce which setups are genuine. Training you to spot a trap is exactly as valuable as training you to spot a valid setup — both protect your Practice Capital.

slides.heading: Ambiguous candle
slides.body: A doji or inside bar at a level — no directional signal despite being 'at the right spot'.

slides.heading: False break
slides.body: Price breaks a level intracandle but closes back inside it — the break isn't confirmed.

slides.heading: Counter-trend entry
slides.body: A setup that looks locally valid but goes directly against a strong higher-timeframe trend — one of the most common ways traders lose money chasing a 'perfect-looking' local pattern.

slides.heading: Open space
slides.body: Price sitting between levels with no identifiable structure at all — there's nothing to confirm, so there's nothing to trade.

quiz.question: What makes a doji at a key level a trap rather than a valid Setup 1?
options: Dojis are always bearish
A doji shows indecision — it's not a directional confirming candle
The level itself is invalid
It only applies on the 1H timeframe
quiz.explanation: Component B of Setup 1 requires a directional reversal candle. A doji shows indecision, not confirmation — that's what makes it a trap, not a signal.

quiz.question: What is a 'false break'?
options: A break that closes beyond the level and holds
A break that touches beyond the level intracandle but closes back inside
Any break on a 5M chart
A break with high volume
quiz.explanation: A false break pokes through a level but fails to close beyond it — the break was never confirmed, which is why it's a trap rather than Setup 3's genuine break.

quiz.question: A setup looks valid on the 5M chart but runs directly against a strong 1H trend. What should you do?
options: Take it — the 5M signal is all that matters
Treat it with heavy suspicion as a counter-trend trap and likely skip it
Double your position size to compensate
Ignore the 1H chart entirely
quiz.explanation: A locally clean-looking setup that fights the higher-timeframe trend is one of the most common traps — this is exactly why higher-timeframe context (Course 1, Lesson 3) matters.

items.explanation: A key level with 2+ prior touches, confirmed by a reversal candle right at the level.
A clear higher-timeframe trend retracing to the 61.8% Fib level with a confirming candle — both labels genuinely apply.
A genuine structure break, retested from the correct side, with a confirming candle — both labels genuinely apply.
The 61.8% retracement is one of the two levels Setup 2 watches for a pullback entry.
A genuine break needs a close beyond the prior swing level, not just a wick through it.
A doji at a level shows indecision, not confirmation — No Trade.
The break wasn't confirmed by a close beyond the level — No Trade.
A locally valid-looking setup fighting a strong higher-timeframe trend is a classic trap.
With no identifiable level or structure, there's nothing to confirm — No Trade.
A trend alone, with no level, retracement, or break in play, is not yet a setup.

courses.title: Risk & Money Management
courses.description: Stop Loss and Take Profit, lot size and pip value, the 1% risk rule, and how margin and leverage actually work. Always accessible standalone, independent of course order.

slides.heading: Stop Loss: non-negotiable
slides.body: A Stop Loss (SL) is the price at which you accept you were wrong and exit automatically. Every single trade in TradeWise requires one before it locks in — there is no version of this app where you can trade without one.

slides.heading: Take Profit
slides.body: A Take Profit (TP) is the price at which you exit having been right. Setting it in advance — before you see the outcome — is what keeps a plan a plan instead of an emotional decision made mid-trade.

slides.heading: Why both are set before the chart plays
slides.body: TradeWise's core mechanic locks in SL and TP before the outcome plays out — exactly like real trading, where you don't get to change your exit after seeing what happens next.

quiz.question: What is a Stop Loss?
options: The price at which you exit having been right
The price at which you exit accepting you were wrong, set in advance
A bonus reward for a winning trade
An optional setting you can skip if confident
quiz.explanation: A Stop Loss is your predetermined exit if the trade goes against you — non-negotiable and required on every trade.

quiz.question: Why does TradeWise require SL and TP to be set before the chart plays, not after?
options: To make the game harder for no reason
To train real decision-making under uncertainty, the same as live trading
Because the app can't calculate them afterward
It doesn't — you can adjust them anytime
quiz.explanation: Setting exits in advance is what separates a disciplined pre-hoc decision from an emotional reaction to price already having moved.

quiz.question: What is a Take Profit?
options: The price at which you exit having been right, set in advance
A stop loss with a different name
The maximum lot size allowed
A leverage setting
quiz.explanation: Take Profit is your predetermined exit target on the winning side — set before you see the outcome.

slides.heading: What a lot size controls
slides.body: Lot size determines how much money moves per pip of price movement. A bigger lot size means bigger swings in your Practice Capital for the same price move — it's the volume dial on your risk.

slides.heading: Worked example: pip value
slides.body: 0.01 lots on EUR/USD ≈ $0.10 per pip. So a 50-pip move against a 0.01 lot position costs about $5. Scale that up: 0.10 lots at 50 pips costs about $50.

slides.heading: Why this isn't optional maths
slides.body: Every lot size decision has a real, calculable dollar consequence on your $500 starting Practice Capital. This is exactly why TradeWise shows you the live risk % before you can lock in a trade.

quiz.question: What does lot size primarily control?
options: The direction of the trade
How much money moves per pip of price movement
The timeframe you're trading on
Your TradePoints balance
quiz.explanation: Lot size is the volume dial — it scales how many dollars each pip of movement is worth.

quiz.question: Roughly what is the pip value of 0.01 lots on EUR/USD?
options: $0.10 per pip
$10 per pip
$1.00 per pip
$100 per pip
quiz.explanation: 0.01 lots (a 'micro lot') on EUR/USD is approximately $0.10 per pip.

quiz.question: At 0.01 lots, roughly what would a 50-pip stop loss cost if hit?
quiz.explanation: 50 pips × $0.10/pip ≈ $5 — a small, controlled loss on a $500 account, which is the point of trading small lot sizes.

slides.heading: The rule itself
slides.body: Risk no more than 1% of your Practice Capital on any single trade. On a $500 account, that's $5 maximum risk per trade — regardless of how confident you feel.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.body: $500 account. 1% risk = $5. Your Stop Loss is 50 pips away. At $0.10/pip (0.01 lots), 50 pips = $5 risked. That's your maximum lot size for this trade: 0.01 lots.

slides.heading: Why 1% instead of 'whatever feels right'
slides.body: At 1% risk, it takes many consecutive losses in a row to meaningfully damage your account — giving your edge time to play out. At 10% risk per trade, a short losing streak can wipe you out before your edge ever gets a fair test.

quiz.question: On a $500 Practice Capital account, what is 1% risk in dollars?
quiz.explanation: 1% of $500 is $5 — the maximum you'd risk on a single trade under the 1% rule.

quiz.question: Your account is $500, your SL is 50 pips away, and pip value at 0.01 lots is $0.10/pip. What's the max lot size that keeps risk at 1% ($5)?
options: 0.001 lots
0.01 lots
0.10 lots
1.00 lots
quiz.explanation: 50 pips × $0.10/pip (0.01 lots) = $5 risked — exactly 1% of $500. That's the correct lot size for this SL distance.

quiz.question: Why does the 1% rule matter more than 'trading with conviction'?
options: It doesn't — conviction should always override sizing
It lets your edge survive a normal losing streak instead of being wiped out by one
It guarantees a profit over time
It's only a suggestion, not a real constraint
quiz.explanation: Small, consistent risk per trade means a losing streak — which will happen even with a real edge — doesn't end your account before that edge has time to prove out.

slides.heading: What leverage means
slides.body: Leverage lets you control a larger position than your capital alone would allow. It amplifies outcomes in both directions — the same 50-pip move produces a bigger dollar swing at higher leverage.

slides.heading: What margin actually is
slides.body: Margin is collateral held against your open position, not a fee charged to you. It's returned when the position closes — it just can't be used for anything else while the trade is open.

slides.heading: Why TradeWise starts at 1:10
slides.body: Low leverage means smaller amplification while you're still building the habit of correct position sizing. Higher leverage tiers unlock later, gated by TradePoints earned through disciplined play — not by account balance alone.

slides.heading: What a margin call is
slides.body: A margin call happens when losses eat too far into your available capital to support open positions — the broker (or in TradeWise, the simulation) starts closing things down to protect what's left. Correct position sizing is how you avoid ever seeing one.

quiz.question: What does leverage do?
options: Guarantees profit on every trade
Amplifies outcomes — both gains and losses — relative to your capital
Removes the need for a Stop Loss
Only applies to Stock trading
quiz.explanation: Leverage lets you control a bigger position with the same capital, which amplifies both wins and losses proportionally.

quiz.question: What is margin?
options: A fee taken from every trade
Collateral held against an open position, returned when it closes
A bonus for high-leverage trades
Another word for Stop Loss
quiz.explanation: Margin is collateral, not a cost — it's tied up while the position is open and released when it closes.

quiz.question: Why does TradeWise start every user at 1:10 leverage instead of higher?
options: Higher leverage isn't technically possible
Lower leverage limits amplification while the habit of correct sizing is still being built
1:10 is a legal maximum everywhere
It has nothing to do with learning — it's arbitrary
quiz.explanation: Starting low keeps early mistakes small while position-sizing discipline is still developing. Higher leverage unlocks later, earned through TradePoints.

items.explanation: A Stop Loss is your predetermined exit accepting you were wrong — set before the trade plays out.
Take Profit is your predetermined exit target if the trade goes your way.
Lot size scales how many dollars each pip of movement is worth.
At 0.01 lots on EUR/USD, each pip is worth roughly $0.10.
Margin is collateral held against an open position — returned when it closes.
Leverage lets you control a bigger position, amplifying gains and losses alike.
Risking no more than 1% per trade means a losing streak doesn't end the account.
50 pips × $0.10/pip = $5, which is exactly 1% of a $500 account — correct sizing.
At 0.10 lots, the same 50-pip SL now risks $50 — 10% of the account, ten times the 1% rule.
A margin call is the simulation protecting remaining capital once losses eat too far into it.

courses.title: Trading Plans & Discipline
courses.description: Why a plan beats improvisation, the three questions every plan answers, the discipline of No Trade, and a plain-language read on the Career Readiness Rating.

lessons.title: Why a Trading Plan Removes Emotion

slides.heading: The problem a plan solves
slides.body: Decisions made in the moment, under uncertainty, with money at stake, are vulnerable to fear and excitement. A plan made in advance — when you're calm — is what you fall back on when you're not.

slides.heading: A plan isn't a prediction
slides.body: A trading plan doesn't predict what the market will do. It predicts what you will do in response to specific, pre-defined conditions — which is the only thing you actually control.

quiz.question: What problem does a trading plan primarily solve?
options: It predicts future price movement
It replaces emotional in-the-moment decisions with pre-committed ones
It guarantees a winning trade
It removes the need for a Stop Loss
quiz.explanation: A plan is a pre-commitment device — it gives you something calm to follow instead of an emotional reaction in the moment.

quiz.question: What does a good trading plan actually predict?
options: What the market will do next
What you will do given specific pre-defined conditions
Your exact profit for the month
Nothing — plans are symbolic only
quiz.explanation: You can't control the market, but a plan lets you pre-commit to your own response to conditions you define in advance.

quiz.question: When is a trading plan created?
options: In the middle of a losing trade
In advance, when you're calm and not under pressure
Only after a big win, to celebrate
It's created automatically by the app for you
quiz.explanation: A plan is written in advance, precisely so it's available to lean on later when emotion is running high.

slides.heading: What do I trade?
slides.body: Which instrument, which setups, which timeframes. Being specific here prevents chasing whatever looks exciting in the moment.

slides.heading: When do I trade?
slides.body: Which sessions, which conditions, and — just as importantly — when you don't trade at all (no clear setup, tired, tilted after a loss).

slides.heading: How much do I risk?
slides.body: Your per-trade risk % (the 1% rule from Course 3) and your session risk budget — the ceiling on total risk you'll take in one sitting, win or lose.

quiz.question: What are the three questions a trading plan answers?
options: What to trade, when to trade, how much to risk
How much profit, how many trades, what colour theme
Who to trade with, where to trade, why to trade
What time zone, what currency, what broker
quiz.explanation: A trading plan answers what you trade, when you trade (and when you don't), and how much you risk.

quiz.question: Why does 'when do I trade' also include 'when I don't trade'?
options: It doesn't — you should always be in a position
Knowing your no-trade conditions (tired, tilted, no clear setup) is as important as knowing your entry conditions
The app forces trades on a schedule
Timing never actually matters
quiz.explanation: A plan that only defines entries is incomplete — defining when to stand aside protects you from the most common source of losses: trading when you shouldn't.

quiz.question: What does 'how much do I risk' refer to in a trading plan?
options: Your total account balance
Your per-trade risk % and your total session risk budget
The number of TradePoints you own
Your leverage tier
quiz.explanation: This question covers both the 1% per-trade rule and a session-level ceiling on cumulative risk taken.

slides.heading: Overtrading is the top cause of retail losses
slides.body: New traders take a position on every setup because sitting out feels like wasted time. In reality, the most disciplined traders skip the majority of potential setups they see.

slides.heading: Why No Trade is scored, not just allowed
slides.body: TradeWise awards points for a correct No Trade call, and never penalises an incorrect No Trade (skipping a valid setup) — because sitting out is always the safer error to make.

slides.heading: No Trade is a skill, not an absence of one
slides.body: Recognising 'this isn't a real setup' requires the same pattern knowledge as recognising a valid one. It's an active decision, not a default.

quiz.question: Why is overtrading described as the top cause of retail trading losses?
options: Because trading is inherently unprofitable
Because traders take positions on setups that aren't actually valid, out of a feeling that inaction wastes opportunity
Because brokers charge fees per trade
It isn't — overtrading is a myth
quiz.explanation: The instinct that 'not trading' is wasted time leads traders into low-quality setups they'd otherwise skip — this is the single most cited driver of retail losses.

quiz.question: How does TradeWise score an incorrect No Trade (skipping a setup that was actually valid)?
options: Large point penalty
Zero points lost — sitting out is always the safer error
Automatic account blow-up
Same penalty as a losing trade
quiz.explanation: Skipping a valid setup costs you the upside, but never costs points — the app is deliberately built to never punish caution more than it punishes recklessness.

quiz.question: Is correctly identifying 'No Trade' considered a real trading skill?
options: No — it's just doing nothing
Yes — it requires the same pattern recognition as spotting a valid setup, applied to recognising when one is absent
Only at Advanced level
Only in Arcade Mode, not Career Mode
quiz.explanation: Recognising the absence of a valid setup uses the same underlying knowledge as recognising a valid one — it's an active skill, not a passive default.

slides.heading: The Career Readiness Rating, in plain language
slides.body: A 0–100 score built from your win rate, correct No-Trade rate, risk consistency, and how many sessions you've completed. It's a mirror on your practice quality — nothing more.

slides.heading: What it is not
slides.body: It is never a qualification, a guarantee, or a signal that you're ready to trade with real money. Every place this score appears in the app carries that same disclaimer, deliberately.

slides.heading: Why the labels matter
slides.body: Early Stage, Developing, Progressing, Practice-Ready — the labels describe practice quality, not permission. Even 'Practice-Ready' users are told explicitly: this reflects simulated performance only.

quiz.question: What does the Career Readiness Rating measure?
options: Whether you're ready to trade live with real money
Your simulated practice quality — win rate, No-Trade accuracy, risk consistency, sessions completed
Your TradePoints balance
Your leverage tier
quiz.explanation: It's a composite of practice-quality signals — never a live-trading qualification.

quiz.question: What does the 'Practice-Ready' label mean?
options: You are certified to trade with real money
Your simulated practice performance has reached a high standard — the label always carries a disclaimer that this reflects practice only
You've unlocked the highest leverage tier automatically
Nothing — it's purely cosmetic
quiz.explanation: Even at the top label, the app is explicit that this reflects simulated practice performance only, never a real-money readiness guarantee.

quiz.question: Which of these does NOT feed into the Career Readiness Rating?
options: Win rate over recent trades
Correct No-Trade rate
Your account's cosmetic chart theme
Risk consistency across trades
quiz.explanation: Cosmetic purchases like chart themes have zero bearing on the score — it's built entirely from trading behaviour and outcomes.

items.explanation: A genuine, complete confluence setup — this is a Trade, not a skip.
Missing the confirming component — this is correctly a No Trade.
With no identifiable structure, there's nothing to confirm — No Trade.
All three components present and confirmed — a valid Trade.
A counter-trend trap — correctly skipped as No Trade.
An unconfirmed, still-forming pattern calls for waiting, not acting early.
All of Setup 2's components are present — a valid Trade.
A false break, not a genuine retest — correctly No Trade.

courses.title: Multi-Timeframe Mastery & Advanced Strategies
courses.price: $6.99 one-time, or included with TradeWise Pro
courses.description: The final two confluence setups, the advanced trap library, session risk budgeting and expectancy, and a primer on the strategy frameworks behind the Strategies Pack.

slides.heading: The components
slides.body: Component A: a key level visible on the 1H chart. Component B: a market structure shift on the 5M chart right at that 1H level. Component C: a candlestick confirmation on the 5M chart.

slides.heading: Valid buy / valid sell
slides.body: Valid BUY: 1H key support, plus a 5M structure shift upward at that level, plus a 5M bullish candle. Valid SELL: 1H key resistance, plus a 5M downward structure shift, plus a 5M bearish candle.

slides.heading: The trap version
slides.body: The 1H level is genuinely there, but the 5M structure hasn't actually shifted yet — price is still making lower highs against 1H support, for example. Correct call: No Trade, wait for the shift to actually happen.

quiz.question: What are the three components of Setup 4?
options: A 1H key level, a 5M structure shift at that level, and a 5M confirming candle
Two Fibonacci levels and a volume spike
A doji and a moving average cross
Three consecutive 1H candles
quiz.explanation: Setup 4 combines a higher-timeframe level with a lower-timeframe structure shift and confirmation — true multi-timeframe agreement.

quiz.question: Price is at 1H support, but the 5M chart is still making lower highs with no structure shift yet. What's correct?
options: Buy immediately — the 1H level is enough on its own
No Trade — wait for the 5M structure to actually shift
Sell — lower highs mean continuation down
Increase lot size to compensate for uncertainty
quiz.explanation: Setup 4 needs all three components. A 1H level alone, without a 5M structure shift, is the trap version — patience is the correct call.

quiz.question: Why is Setup 4 introduced only after Setups 1–3?
options: It uses a completely unrelated skill set
It builds directly on structure-reading (Course 1) and structure breaks (Setup 3), combined across two timeframes at once
It's easier than the earlier setups
There's no particular reason
quiz.explanation: Multi-timeframe confluence layers structure-reading and break/retest skills across two timeframes simultaneously — it depends on the earlier setups being solid first.

slides.heading: The components
slides.body: Component A: a narrowing range — lower highs and higher lows — visible over 10+ candles on the 5M chart. Component B: a breakout candle closing outside the compression with a body at least 1.5× the average body size of the compression period. Component C: the breakout direction aligns with the 15M trend or momentum.

slides.heading: Valid buy / valid sell
slides.body: Valid BUY: compression, then a bullish breakout candle closing above the range, with the 15M trend up or neutral. Valid SELL: compression, then a bearish breakout closing below the range, with the 15M confirming.

slides.heading: The trap version
slides.body: A breakout wick pokes outside the range but the candle doesn't close beyond it — or the breakout fires directly against a strong 1H trend. Both are correctly No Trade.

quiz.question: What defines the 'compression' in Compression Breakout?
options: A single large candle
A narrowing range — lower highs and higher lows — over 10+ candles
Any sideways price action, regardless of shape
A gap between two candles
quiz.explanation: Compression specifically means the range is narrowing candle over candle — lower highs meeting higher lows, squeezing toward a point.

quiz.question: What size does the breakout candle's body need to be, relative to the compression period?
options: Any size at all
At least 1.5× the average body size of the compression candles
Exactly the same size as the previous candle
Smaller than the compression candles
quiz.explanation: The breakout needs real conviction behind it — a body at least 1.5× the compression period's average, not just a marginal push outside the range.

quiz.question: A breakout candle wicks outside the compression range but closes back inside it. What's correct?
options: Trade the breakout direction anyway
No Trade — the close never confirmed the breakout
Always trade against the wick
Increase lot size since volatility is rising
quiz.explanation: Component B requires a close outside the range, not just a wick. Without that close, it's the trap version of Setup 5.

slides.heading: False break / liquidity sweep, revisited
slides.body: At this level, false breaks get sharper: price can sweep through a level aggressively — designed to trigger stop losses clustered just beyond it — before reversing hard the other way.

slides.heading: Counter-trend traps
slides.body: A setup with every local component present, but positioned directly against a strong, well-established higher-timeframe trend. These are the most convincing traps precisely because the local pattern is genuinely clean.

slides.heading: News-simulation spikes
slides.body: A sharp, fast directional move with no structural basis — no level, no break, no compression. It's volatility without a story. Trading it as if it were a valid setup is a Stage 3+ trap.

quiz.question: What is a liquidity sweep?
options: A slow, gradual price drift
An aggressive push through a level — often to trigger clustered stop losses — before reversing
A type of candlestick pattern
A guaranteed reversal signal
quiz.explanation: A liquidity sweep is a sharp move through a level, frequently understood as clearing out stop losses sitting just beyond it, before price reverses.

quiz.question: Why are counter-trend traps described as 'the most convincing'?
options: Because they never actually look valid
Because the local pattern genuinely is clean — it's only the higher-timeframe context that makes it a trap
Because they only occur on weekends
Because they always involve a doji
quiz.explanation: The local setup can be textbook-correct in isolation — what makes it a trap is fighting the higher-timeframe trend, which is easy to miss if you only look at the immediate chart.

quiz.question: What structurally distinguishes a news-simulation spike from a valid Setup 5 breakout?
options: Nothing — they look identical
The spike has no compression, level, or structural basis behind the move
It only happens on EUR/USD
It always aligns with the 15M trend
quiz.explanation: A valid breakout has a structural setup behind it (compression). A news-spike is volatility with no such basis — trading it as a setup is the trap.

slides.heading: Beyond per-trade risk: the session budget
slides.body: The 1% rule caps a single trade. A session risk budget caps how much you're willing to risk across an entire sitting — a warning triggers if any single trade exceeds 2% of Practice Capital, even though it's not blocked outright.

slides.heading: What an R-multiple is
slides.body: An R-multiple expresses a trade's result relative to what you risked. Risk $5 (1R) and make $10, that's a +2R trade. Risk $5 and lose it, that's -1R. Thinking in R lets you compare trades of different sizes fairly.

slides.heading: Expectancy, in one line
slides.body: Expectancy = (win rate × average R won) − (loss rate × average R lost). A positive expectancy system can still have more losing trades than winning ones and be profitable overall — this is why a single loss (or win) never tells the whole story.

quiz.question: What does a session risk budget add on top of the 1% per-trade rule?
options: Nothing — they're the same thing
A ceiling on total risk taken across an entire session, not just one trade
A guarantee against any losses
A higher leverage allowance
quiz.explanation: The 1% rule governs one trade; the session budget governs the cumulative risk across everything you do in one sitting.

quiz.question: You risk $5 (1R) and the trade closes at +$15 profit. What R-multiple is that?
quiz.explanation: $15 profit against $5 risked is 3× the risk — a +3R result.

quiz.question: Can a trading system with more losing trades than winning trades still be profitable overall?
options: No — win rate above 50% is always required
Yes — if the average size of wins (in R) sufficiently outweighs the average size of losses
Only if leverage is very high
Only in Arcade Mode
quiz.explanation: Expectancy depends on win rate AND average R per win/loss together — a system that wins less often but wins bigger can still have positive expectancy overall.

slides.heading: Why frameworks, not just setups
slides.body: The 5 core setups are individual patterns. A strategy framework is a broader lens for reading the market that several setups can sit inside — this lesson is a primer, not the full depth (see the Strategies Pack for that).

slides.heading: ICT-inspired concepts
slides.body: A family of ideas centred on liquidity — where clusters of stop losses likely sit, and how price is drawn toward them before reversing. You've already seen a piece of this in the liquidity sweep trap.

slides.heading: SMC (Smart Money Concepts) structure
slides.body: A framework built around identifying where larger participants are likely positioned, using structure breaks and order-flow-style reasoning rather than indicators.

slides.heading: Momentum continuation
slides.body: A framework focused on trading in the direction of established momentum rather than looking for reversals — the opposite instinct to trading every level as a turning point.

quiz.question: What is a 'strategy framework' as distinct from one of the 5 core setups?
options: Exactly the same thing, just a different name
A broader lens for reading the market that multiple individual setups can operate within
A type of candlestick pattern
A leverage tier
quiz.explanation: A framework is a bigger-picture approach to reading the market — setups are specific patterns; a framework is the lens you view many patterns through.

quiz.question: Which core concept from this course connects directly to ICT-inspired thinking?
options: Compression breakout body size
The liquidity sweep / false break trap
The 1% risk rule
Candlestick colour
quiz.explanation: Liquidity sweeps — price pushing through a level to clear out stop losses before reversing — are a foundational ICT-inspired idea you already met as a trap pattern.

quiz.question: What does 'momentum continuation' focus on, in contrast to reversal-based setups like Setup 1?
options: Trading in the direction of established momentum rather than looking for turning points
Only trading during news spikes
Ignoring all structure entirely
Trading exclusively on the 1-minute timeframe
quiz.explanation: Where Setup 1 looks for reversals at a level, momentum continuation looks the other way — trading with an already-established directional move.

items.explanation: 1H level, 5M structure shift, and 5M confirmation all present together.
Compression, a conviction breakout candle, and 15M alignment together.
An aggressive sweep through clustered stops, followed by reversal — not a valid break.
The local pattern is clean, but fights a well-established higher-timeframe trend.
Volatility without any structural basis — not a Setup 5 breakout.
Under the 2% single-trade warning threshold — within budget.
Above the 2% single-trade threshold — a risk-budget warning case.
$10 profit against $5 risked is twice the risk — a +2R result.
A full loss of the risked amount is exactly -1R.
ICT-inspired thinking centres on where liquidity (stop losses) clusters and how price is drawn to it.
SMC reasons about structure breaks as evidence of where larger participants are positioned.
This framework trades in the direction of existing momentum rather than hunting reversals.
